entries.lesson_core_move: Set up the one-sided Laplace transform as $X(s)=\int_{0^-}^{\infty} x(t)e^{-st}\,dt$, identifying the lower limit, exponential weighting, and complex $s$-domain representation used for causal signal and system analysis.

sections.section_title: Identifying the Time-Domain Signal and $s$-Domain Transform

prompt_blocks.text: For $x(t)=u(t)$, which choice is the correct one-sided setup for $X(s)$?

answer_explanation_blocks.text: The correct setup keeps the one-sided lower limit $0^-$, uses the signal $u(t)$ directly, and applies the standard kernel $e^{-st}$ once in the integral.

prompt_blocks.text: For $x(t)=2u(t-1)$, identify the correct one-sided Laplace setup expression for $X(s)$.

answer_explanation_blocks.text: The delayed step signal is substituted directly, while the transform convention stays one-sided with bounds $0^-$ to $\infty$ and kernel $e^{-st}$; only the lower bound and exponent sign remain fixed.

sections.section_title: Setting the One-Sided Integration Limits

prompt_blocks.text: For $x(t)=e^{-3t}u(t)$, choose the correct one-sided Laplace setup for $X(s)$.

answer_explanation_blocks.text: $x(t)=e^{-3t}u(t)$ is causal, so the correct one-sided interval starts at $0^-$. The bilateral bounds in A are incorrect for a one-sided setup, B removes the origin-inclusive notation, D incorrectly truncates the upper limit, and E reverses bounds.

prompt_blocks.text: For $x(t)=4e^{-t}u(t-2)$, identify the correct one-sided transform setup.

answer_explanation_blocks.text: The delayed step remains a causal signal, so the one-sided interval is still $0^-$ to $\infty$ with the same transform kernel and delayed-step factor in the integrand. Choice B changes the lower limit to a nonzero start, choice A uses bilateral bounds, choice D truncates the interval, and choice E is a reversed-bound typo.

sections.section_title: Applying the Exponential Weighting Factor

prompt_blocks.text: Choose the correct one-sided setup for $x(t)=5e^{-2t}u(t)$ after applying the exponential weighting term.

answer_explanation_blocks.text: Start from $X(s)=\\int_{0^-}^{\\infty}x(t)e^{-st}\\,dt$ and substitute $x(t)=5e^{-2t}u(t)$ directly. The causal limit stays at $0^-$, and the kernel remains $e^{-st}$; any sign flip, missing kernel, time reversal, or denominator form is incorrect for this step.

prompt_blocks.text: Write the correct one-sided weighted-integral form for $x(t)=\\frac{1}{2}e^{3t}u(t)$.

answer_explanation_blocks.text: Apply the definition and substitute $x(t)=\\frac{1}{2}e^{3t}u(t)$: $X(s)=\\int_{0^-}^{\\infty}\\left(\\frac{1}{2}e^{3t}u(t)\\right)e^{-st}\\,dt$. This can be combined to $\\frac{1}{2}e^{-(s-3)t}u(t)$ inside the same one-sided bounds. Changing the kernel sign, reversing time, dropping $e^{-st}$, or changing the coefficient breaks the setup.

sections.section_title: Writing the Complete One-Sided Laplace Transform Setup

prompt_blocks.text: Select the complete one-sided setup for the Laplace transform when $x(t)=u(t)$.

answer_explanation_blocks.text: The one-sided definition is $X(s)=\int_{0^-}^{\infty}x(t)e^{-st}\,dt$, so for $x(t)=u(t)$ the complete setup is $X(s)=\int_{0^-}^{\infty}u(t)e^{-st}\,dt$. Bilateral bounds, reversed kernel sign, finite upper limits, or swapping the transform and time variable labels are all inconsistent with this step.

prompt_blocks.text: Choose the correct one-sided setup for $x(t)=3u(t)$. (No evaluation, setup only.)

answer_explanation_blocks.text: Use the same one-sided template, substitute $x(t)$, and keep the causal interval and kernel unchanged. For $x(t)=3u(t)$, the setup is $X(s)=\int_{0^-}^{\infty}3u(t)e^{-st}\,dt$. Missing $0^-$, changing bounds to finite limits, or swapping the transform/symbol roles (for example $X(t)=\cdots$) does not match the required complete setup.

entries.lesson_core_move: Apply the $0^-$ convention when setting up one-sided Laplace transforms so discontinuities and impulses at $t=0$ are included consistently in causal signal analysis.

sections.section_title: Setting a One-Sided Laplace Integral from $0^-$

prompt_blocks.text: For $x(t)=u(t)+3u(t-2)$, choose the correct one-sided setup for $X(s)$ using the $0^-$ convention.

answer_explanation_blocks.text: This is a causal-signal setup, so the lower limit must remain $0^-$ and the transform stays one-sided from $0^-$ to $\infty$.
Substitute the full signal $x(t)$ exactly as written: $u(t)+3u(t-2)$; then place it in the same template with $e^{-st}$ intact.
Option $C$ swaps the time argument with the transform variable, and option $E$ drops the delay term, both of which break the direct setup rule for this step.

prompt_blocks.text: For $x(t)=2u(t)-u(t-3)$, choose the correct one-sided setup for $X(s)$.

answer_explanation_blocks.text: The signal is causal, so the lower limit is still $0^-$ and the integral must remain one-sided.
Option $A$ is incomplete because it omits the exponential weighting factor, and option $E$ changes the delayed branch from $u(t-3)$ to $u(t)$.
Option $B$ uses bilateral bounds and option $C$ swaps the transform variable label, so both violate the one-sided setup rule in this section.

sections.section_title: Recognizing Signals That Change at $t=0$

prompt_blocks.text: For $x(t)=\begin{cases}4,&t<0\0,&0\le t<1\3,&t\ge 1\end{cases}$, select the correct one-sided Laplace setup that keeps only causal support and handles the origin jump correctly.

answer_explanation_blocks.text: Only causal time is integrated in one-sided Laplace setup, so the branch $t<0$ is excluded by the lower limit $0^-$. A finite jump at $t=0$ does not add a separate non-integral finite-area term in this setup, and $0^-$ is used to keep origin support conventions consistent for causal analysis.

prompt_blocks.text: For $x(t)=\begin{cases}-2,&t<0\1,&0\le t<2\-1,&t\ge 2\end{cases}$, which setup is correct for the one-sided transform question model in this step?

answer_explanation_blocks.text: The step is causal, so integration starts at $0^-$ and excludes the $t<0$ branch. Keep both causal subintervals, $[0,2)$ and $[2,\infty)$, and do not convert the jump at $t=0$ into an extra integral term or an impulse unless the signal is explicitly impulsive at the origin.

sections.section_title: Including an Impulse at $t=0$

prompt_blocks.text: Choose the correct one-sided transform setup for $x(t)=3\delta(t)+u(t)$.

answer_explanation_blocks.text: Use the one-sided template first: $X(s)=\int_{0^-}^{\infty}x(t)e^{-st}\,dt$, then substitute $x(t)=3\delta(t)+u(t)$. The impulse at the lower endpoint contributes $3$, while the step term remains in the causal integral.

prompt_blocks.text: For $x(t)=4\delta(t)+u(t-1)$, pick the correct one-sided Laplace setup expression.

answer_explanation_blocks.text: Start from $\int_{0^-}^{\infty}$, not $0^+$. The $4\delta(t)$ term is evaluated at the origin and adds $4$, while $u(t-1)$ is causal but begins at $t=1$, so it is carried as an unchanged step term under the one-sided transform setup (or equivalently simplified to $\int_{1}^{\infty}e^{-st}\,dt$).

sections.section_title: Excluding Signal Behavior Before $t=0$

prompt_blocks.text: For $x(t)=-3$ when $t<0$ and $x(t)=2e^{-2t}$ when $t\ge0$, choose the correct one-sided setup for $X(s)$.

answer_explanation_blocks.text: Use the causal branch only: the one-sided transform starts at $0^-$ and includes only the $t\ge0$ expression.
Choice $A$ is bilateral. Choice $B$ incorrectly adds the pre-origin branch. Choice $C$ replaces the causal branch with an impulse term, and choice $E$ swaps the time and transform variables.

prompt_blocks.text: For $x(t)=4$ when $t<0$ and $x(t)=t+1$ when $t\ge0$, choose the correct one-sided integral setup for $X(s)$.

answer_explanation_blocks.text: Keep the lower limit at $0^-$ and use only the post-origin branch $t+1$; that is the causal setup rule for this step.
Choice $A$ incorrectly adds the $t<0$ branch. Choice $B$ uses an impulse substitute, choice $C$ is bilateral, and choice $D$ changes the endpoint to $0^+$.

entries.lesson_core_move: Compute the one-sided Laplace transform of $e^{-at}u(t)$ from the $0^-$-to-$\infty$ definition, producing $X(s)=1/(s+a)$ with convergence condition $\operatorname{Re}(s)>-a$ as the base exponential transform pair.

sections.section_title: Setting Up the One-Sided Integral for $e^{-at}u(t)$

prompt_blocks.text: Which expression correctly sets up the one-sided Laplace transform integral for $x(t)=e^{-t}u(t)$?

answer_explanation_blocks.text: The one-sided definition uses lower limit $0^-$ and includes the factor $e^{-st}$, so substituting $x(t)=e^{-t}u(t)$ gives the setup in choice A.

prompt_blocks.text: For $x(t)=e^{-4t}u(t)$, which expression is the correct one-sided setup after combining the exponential factors?

answer_explanation_blocks.text: Using $\int_{0^-}^{\infty}x(t)e^{-st}\,dt$ with $x(t)=e^{-4t}u(t)$ gives $e^{-4t}e^{-st}=e^{-(s+4)t}$ over the one-sided interval.

sections.section_title: Evaluating the Integral to Obtain $1/(s+a)$

prompt_blocks.text: Evaluate $\mathcal{L}_+\{e^{-4t}u(t)\}$ from the one-sided integral and simplify the result.

answer_explanation_blocks.text: The one-sided integral is $\int_{0^-}^{\infty} e^{-(s+4)t}\,dt$. The antiderivative is $-\frac{1}{s+4}e^{-(s+4)t}$, and with $\operatorname{Re}(s)>-4$, the upper-limit term is $0$, leaving $\frac{1}{s+4}$.

prompt_blocks.text: Evaluate $\mathcal{L}_+\{e^{-7t}u(t)\}$ from the one-sided integral and simplify the result.

answer_explanation_blocks.text: Use $\mathcal{L}_+\{e^{-7t}u(t)\}=\int_{0^-}^{\infty}e^{-(s+7)t}\,dt$. Evaluating $-\frac{1}{s+7}e^{-(s+7)t}$ at the bounds gives $0-\left(-\frac{1}{s+7}\right)=\frac{1}{s+7}$ when $\operatorname{Re}(s)>-7$.

sections.section_title: Determining the Convergence Condition $\operatorname{Re}(s)>-a$

prompt_blocks.text: Find the region of convergence for $\mathcal{L}_+\{e^{-4t}u(t)\}=\frac{1}{s+4}$.

answer_explanation_blocks.text: The upper-limit term contains $e^{-(s+4)t}$, which vanishes as $t\to\infty$ only when $\operatorname{Re}(s+4)>0$.

prompt_blocks.text: Find the region of convergence for $\mathcal{L}_+\{e^{3t}u(t)\}=\frac{1}{s-3}$.

answer_explanation_blocks.text: Since $e^{3t}=e^{-(-3)t}$, this matches the base form with $a=-3$. The tail term vanishes when $\operatorname{Re}(s+a)>0$.

sections.section_title: Reading Specific Exponential Signals as $1/(s+a)$ Pairs

prompt_blocks.text: Identify the one-sided Laplace transform pair for $e^{-6t}u(t)$, including its ROC.

answer_explanation_blocks.text: Match $e^{-6t}u(t)$ to the template $e^{-at}u(t)$, so $a=6$.
Substituting $a=6$ gives the denominator $s+6$ and the ROC $\operatorname{Re}(s)>-6$.

prompt_blocks.text: Identify the one-sided Laplace transform pair for $e^{2t}u(t)$, including its ROC.

answer_explanation_blocks.text: Rewrite $e^{2t}u(t)$ as $e^{-(-2)t}u(t)$, so this still matches the template with $a=-2$.
The denominator changes to $s+a=s-2$, and the ROC condition $\operatorname{Re}(s)>-a$ becomes $\operatorname{Re}(s)>2$.

entries.lesson_title: Laplace Transform of the Unit Step
entries.lesson_core_move: Derive the one-sided Laplace transform of $u(t)$ as $U(s)=1/s$ by treating it as the $a=0$ case of $e^{-at}u(t)$ and checking the $\operatorname{Re}(s)>0$ convergence condition.

sections.lesson_title: Laplace Transform of the Unit Step
sections.section_title: Computing the Unit Step Transform as the $a=0$ Exponential Case

prompt_blocks.text: Use the one-sided definition to compute $X(s)=\mathcal{L}\{x(t)\}$ for $x(t)=2u(t)$.
Report the transform and the convergence condition.

answer_explanation_blocks.text: Apply the one-sided form $X(s)=\int_{0^-}^{\infty}x(t)e^{-st}\,dt$.
Substitute $x(t)=2u(t)$ and use $u(t)=1$ for $t\ge 0$, giving $X(s)=\int_{0^-}^{\infty}2e^{-st}\,dt=\int_{0}^{\infty}2e^{-st}\,dt$.
The ROC condition is required for the upper-limit term to vanish; without it the integral does not converge.

prompt_blocks.text: Compute the one-sided Laplace transform of $x(t)=-3u(t)$, and include the ROC in the same expression.
Keep the one-sided limit explicitly in the setup.

answer_explanation_blocks.text: Start from $X(s)=\int_{0^-}^{\infty}x(t)e^{-st}\,dt$ with $x(t)=-3u(t)$.
The one-sided lower limit $0^-$ keeps the causal convention; missing the sign or ROC condition are the most common errors.

sections.lesson_title: Laplace Transform of the Unit Step
sections.section_title: Deriving $U(s)=1/s$ from the One-Sided Integral

prompt_blocks.text:
Evaluate the one-sided integral for the unit step and select the correct transform result with its required region of convergence.

$U(s)=\int_{0^-}^{\infty} e^{-st}\,dt$

answer_explanation_blocks.text: Use the antiderivative $\int e^{-st}\,dt=-\frac{1}{s}e^{-st}$. At the lower bound, $\left.-\frac{1}{s}e^{-st}\right|_{t\to0^-}= -\frac{1}{s}\cdot 1$. At the upper bound, $\lim_{b\to\infty}(-\frac{1}{s}e^{-sb})=0$ only when $\operatorname{Re}(s)>0$, leaving $\frac{1}{s}$.

prompt_blocks.text:
Apply the same one-sided-limit procedure to a scaled step and choose the correct transform with region of convergence.

$U(s)=\int_{0^-}^{\infty} 2e^{-st}\,dt$

answer_explanation_blocks.text: Factor out the scale: $\int 2e^{-st}\,dt=-\frac{2}{s}e^{-st}$. Evaluate from $0^-$ to $\infty$ to get $\lim_{b\to\infty}\left(-\frac{2}{s}e^{-sb}\right)-\left(-\frac{2}{s}\cdot1\right)=\frac{2}{s}$, which is valid when the upper-limit term vanishes for $\operatorname{Re}(s)>0$.

sections.lesson_title: Laplace Transform of the Unit Step
sections.section_title: Checking the $\operatorname{Re}(s)>0$ Convergence Condition

prompt_blocks.text: For the one-sided Laplace integral, select the condition that makes the transform valid.

choice_blocks.text: No restriction on $s$; the integral is bounded for all $s$.

answer_explanation_blocks.text: Set $s=\sigma+j\omega$. Then $e^{-st}=e^{-\sigma t}e^{-j\omega t}$, so convergence depends on $|e^{-\sigma t}|=e^{-\sigma t}$. As $t\to\infty$, the upper-limit term goes to $0$ only if $\sigma>0$, i.e. $\operatorname{Re}(s)>0$.

prompt_blocks.text: This one-sided integral appears in the same convergence-check step. Pick the correct ROC.

answer_explanation_blocks.text: Write the complex shift in the exponent as $(s+2)=\sigma+2+j\omega$. Then the magnitude term is $e^{-(\sigma+2)t}$, so the decay condition is $\sigma+2>0$, or $\operatorname{Re}(s)>-2$. The non-strict bound and imaginary-part-only options are not the convergence requirement.

sections.lesson_title: Laplace Transform of the Unit Step
sections.section_title: Recognizing $1/s$ as the Unit Step Transform Pair

prompt_blocks.text: Match the one-sided $s$-domain pair to its causal time-domain signal.

answer_explanation_blocks.text: The denominator is exactly $s$ with a pole order of one at the origin, so this matches the causal unit-step template from this module.
Option $B$ has the same numerator but the incorrect region tag, option $D$ is a shifted exponential with denominator $s+1$, and option $E$ implies a repeated pole corresponding to $tu(t)$.

prompt_blocks.text: Choose the correct time-domain signal and ROC for the transform.

answer_explanation_blocks.text: Keep the sign and ROC from $U(s)$. A leading minus sign gives $-u(t)$, not $u(t)$. The ROC condition is still the right-half-plane condition for a one-sided causal unit-step family with this denominator form.
Option $C$ changes support to the left half-plane, option $D$ changes the denominator form to $s+1$, and option $E$ adds a repeated-pole pattern that does not match $1/s$.

entries.lesson_title: Laplace Transform of the Unit Impulse
entries.lesson_core_move: Compute the one-sided Laplace transform of $\delta(t)$ by using the $0^-$ convention to include the impulse at the origin and convert it into the constant $s$-domain value $1$.

sections.lesson_title: Laplace Transform of the Unit Impulse
sections.section_title: Applying Sifting to the One-Sided Transform of $\delta(t)$

prompt_blocks.text: Evaluate $\int_{0^-}^{\infty}\delta(u)e^{-su}\,du$ using the one-sided interval convention.

answer_explanation_blocks.text: The lower limit $0^-$ includes the impulse at the origin. Sifting samples $e^{-su}$ at $u=0$, so the integral is $e^{-s\cdot 0}=1$.

prompt_blocks.text: For $X(s)=\mathcal{L}_{+}\{\delta(t)\}$, which expression correctly applies sifting in the one-sided transform integral?

answer_explanation_blocks.text: In $\mathcal{L}_{+}\{\delta(t)\}=\int_{0^-}^{\infty}\delta(t)e^{-st}\,dt$, the impulse samples the multiplier at $t=0$. Because $0^-$ includes that impulse, $X(s)=e^{-s\cdot 0}=1$.

sections.lesson_title: Laplace Transform of the Unit Impulse
sections.section_title: Including the Origin Impulse with the $0^-$ Lower Limit

prompt_blocks.text: For the one-sided Laplace transform, which value comes from using the lower limit $0^-$ for the impulse $\delta(t)$ at the origin?

answer_explanation_blocks.text: The lower limit $0^-$ includes the boundary impulse at $t=0$, so the sifting contribution is kept.

prompt_blocks.text: Which comparison correctly states what happens if the lower limit is changed from $0^-$ to $0^+$ for $\delta(t)$?

answer_explanation_blocks.text: The interval beginning at $0^-$ includes the impulse at the boundary, while the interval beginning at $0^+$ starts after the impulse.

sections.lesson_title: Laplace Transform of the Unit Impulse
sections.section_title: Transforming Scaled Unit Impulses at the Origin

prompt_blocks.text: Find $\mathcal{L}_{+}\{4\delta(t)\}$ using the one-sided Laplace definition.

answer_explanation_blocks.text: Use linearity to pull out the scale factor $4$, then apply the same one-sided impulse result from $0^-$.

prompt_blocks.text: What is $\mathcal{L}_{+}\{\frac{3}{2}\delta(t)\}$?

answer_explanation_blocks.text: The coefficient on $\delta(t)$ comes out of the one-sided Laplace integral, and the impulse at the origin contributes $1$.

entries.lesson_core_move: Determine whether a shifted impulse lies inside the $0^-$-to-$\infty$ one-sided interval, then use sifting to convert $A\delta(t-T)$ into $Ae^{-sT}$ for $T\ge 0$.

sections.section_title: Transforming a Shifted Impulse Inside the One-Sided Interval

prompt_blocks.text: Compute $\mathcal{L}\{4\delta(t-1)\}$.

answer_explanation_blocks.text: For $A\delta(t-T)$ with $T\ge 0$, the one-sided Laplace transform is $Ae^{-sT}$. Here $A=4$ and $T=1$, so the transform is $4e^{-s}$.

prompt_blocks.text: Compute $\mathcal{L}\{6\delta(t-5)\}$.

answer_explanation_blocks.text: The impulse is at $T=5$, which is inside the one-sided interval because $5\ge 0$. Sifting gives the amplitude times $e^{-sT}$, so $6\delta(t-5)$ transforms to $6e^{-5s}$.

sections.section_title: Including Amplitude in a Shifted Impulse Transform

prompt_blocks.text: Compute $\mathcal{L}\{\frac{3}{4}\delta(t-2)\}$.

answer_explanation_blocks.text: For a shifted impulse, $A\delta(t-T)$ transforms to $Ae^{-sT}$ when $T\ge 0$. Here $A=\frac{3}{4}$ and $T=2$, so the amplitude is preserved and the transform is $\frac{3}{4}e^{-2s}$.

prompt_blocks.text: Compute $\mathcal{L}\{-6\delta(t-5)\}$.

answer_explanation_blocks.text: The impulse location is $T=5$, which is inside the one-sided interval because $5\ge 0$. Applying $A\delta(t-T)\to Ae^{-sT}$ with $A=-6$ gives $-6e^{-5s}$.

sections.section_title: Handling an Impulse at the Origin with the $0^-$ Convention

prompt_blocks.text: Using the one-sided Laplace transform with lower limit $0^-$, compute $\mathcal{L}\{-3\delta(t)\}$.

answer_explanation_blocks.text: The $0^-$ lower limit includes an impulse located at $t=0$, so the impulse is not dropped.

prompt_blocks.text: For the one-sided transform defined from $0^-$ to $\infty$, what is $\mathcal{L}\{4\delta(t)\}$?

answer_explanation_blocks.text: With the $0^-$ convention, the origin impulse lies inside the one-sided integration interval.

sections.section_title: Recognizing Shifted Impulses Outside the One-Sided Interval

prompt_blocks.text: Compute $\mathcal{L}\{-2\delta(t+4)\}$ using the one-sided interval $[0^-,\infty)$.

answer_explanation_blocks.text: Rewrite $-2\delta(t+4)$ as $-2\delta(t-(-4))$, so the impulse support point is $T=-4$.
Because $T=-4$ is outside the one-sided interval $[0^-,\infty)$, the impulse contributes nothing to the integral.

prompt_blocks.text: Compute $\mathcal{L}\{4\delta(t+3)\}$ using the one-sided interval $[0^-,\infty)$.

answer_explanation_blocks.text: Rewrite $4\delta(t+3)$ as $4\delta(t-(-3))$, so the impulse support point is $T=-3$.
The condition $T\ge 0$ fails, so this shifted impulse is not inside the one-sided interval $[0^-,\infty)$.

entries.lesson_core_move: Invert basic one-sided Laplace-domain transform pairs into causal time-domain signals by recognizing unit-step, exponential, impulse, and shifted-impulse forms under the $0^-$ convention.

sections.section_title: Inverting the Unit-Step Pair

prompt_blocks.text: What is $L^{-1}(5/s)$ under the one-sided convention?

answer_explanation_blocks.text: This transform is a scaled unit-step pair with numerator constant $5$, so by the one-sided pair rule the inverse is $5u(t)$.
The other options mix up the template: $5/s$ leaves the result in the $s$-domain, $5\delta(t)$ is the impulse form, $5u(t-1)$ is a shifted step, and $-5u(t)$ applies the wrong sign.

prompt_blocks.text: What is $L^{-1}(-4/s)$ under the one-sided convention?

answer_explanation_blocks.text: A negative numerator scales the unit-step inverse directly, so $L^{-1}(-4/s)=-4u(t)$ with one-sided causal support.
$-4/s$, $-4\delta(t)$, and $-4u(t-1)$ all use the wrong template for this cue, while $4u(-t)$ flips support to anti-causal instead of one-sided-causal.

sections.section_title: Inverting One-Sided Exponential Pairs

prompt_blocks.text: Find the inverse one-sided Laplace transform of $X(s)=\frac{5}{s+4}$.

answer_explanation_blocks.text: Match to the template $\mathcal{L}^{-1}\left(\frac{A}{s+a}\right)=Ae^{-at}u(t)$.
Options include common confusions: growth instead of decay, impulse interpretation, time shift at $t=1$, and forgetting $u(t)$.

prompt_blocks.text: Find the inverse one-sided Laplace transform of $X(s)=\frac{7}{s-1}$.

answer_explanation_blocks.text: Use the same pattern with $A/(s+a)$: here $\frac{7}{s-1}=\frac{7}{s+(-1)}$, so $A=7$ and $a=-1$.
The incorrect options either flip the sign on the time exponent, remove causality support, or add an unsupported shift.

sections.section_title: Inverting the Unit-Impulse Pair

prompt_blocks.text: Find $L^{-1}(5)$ under the one-sided convention.

answer_explanation_blocks.text: A constant $X(s)$ term maps directly to a unit impulse in the one-sided inverse pair rule, so $L^{-1}(5)=5\delta(t)$.
$5\delta(t-1)$ adds a shift that is not present, $5u(t)$ is the step pair, $5e^{-t}u(t)$ is the exponential pair, and $\frac{5}{5}\delta(t)$ misapplies the scaling.

prompt_blocks.text: Find $L^{-1}(-3)$ under the one-sided convention.

answer_explanation_blocks.text: A constant transform still maps to the origin impulse, so multiplying by $-3$ gives $L^{-1}(-3)=-3\delta(t)$.
The shifted impulse changes support to $t=1$, the step and exponential forms are template errors, and $-3t$ is a non-impulse algebraic form.

sections.section_title: Inverting Shifted-Impulse Pairs

prompt_blocks.text: Find the inverse one-sided transform of $X(s)=3e^{-2s}$.

answer_explanation_blocks.text: Match $X(s)=3e^{-2s}$ to $A e^{-sT}$ as $A=3$, $T=2$. Because it is a delayed impulse term and $T \ge 0$, the inverse is $x(t)=3\delta(t-2)$.

prompt_blocks.text: Find the inverse one-sided transform of $X(s)=-4e^{-5s}$.

answer_explanation_blocks.text: Again match to $A e^{-sT}$ with $A=-4$ and $T=5$. The rule $L^{-1}(A e^{-sT}) = A\delta(t-T)$ gives $x(t)=-4\delta(t-5)$; this keeps the impulse delayed by a positive $T$ and preserves the negative amplitude.

sections.section_title: Choosing Among Basic One-Sided Transform Pairs

prompt_blocks.text: Choose the inverse of $X(s)=e^{-2s}\left(3+\frac{5}{s+4}\right)$.

answer_explanation_blocks.text: The outer factor is $e^{-2s}$, so apply one-sided delay first: $e^{-2s}F(s) \leftrightarrow f(t-2)u(t-2)$. Here $F(s)=3+\frac{5}{s+4}$.
Split $F(s)$ into standard terms: $3\leftrightarrow 3\delta(t)$ and $\frac{5}{s+4}\leftrightarrow 5e^{-4t}u(t)$, then shift both by $2$.
So the inverse is $3\delta(t-2)+5e^{-4(t-2)}u(t-2)$.

prompt_blocks.text: Choose the inverse of $X(s)=e^{-s}\left(4+\frac{3}{s}\right)$.

answer_explanation_blocks.text: Again, classify by the delay factor first: $e^{-s}\leftrightarrow$ shift by $1$. So delay each base inverse by $t\to t-1$.
Inside $4+\frac{3}{s}$, use $4\leftrightarrow 4\delta(t)$ and $\frac{3}{s}\leftrightarrow 3u(t)$.
The shifted result is therefore $4\delta(t-1)+3u(t-1)$; options that omit the shift, flip support, or change template are incorrect.
